nodes.statement: Test configurations were first introduced in , where the special fiber was required to be normal, and the generalized Futaki invariant was defined in analytic terms. Later in , any degeneration was allowed (indeed instead of a Fano variety, considered test configurations of any given polarized projective variety), and the generalized Futaki invariant was defined in algebraic terms as above. Therefore, in some literature, the generalized Futaki invariant is also called the Donaldson-Futaki invariant. Since in our current note, we will mostly restrict ourselves to a even smaller class (see Definition ) than in Tian's setting, to avoid any confusion, we will only use the terminology in . In different literatures, the definition of the generalized Futaki invariant may differ by a (positive) constant. As we will see, in Definition of K-stability, it is only the sign of the generalized Futaki invariant that matters.

nodes.statement: The most important feature for testing K-stability is that we have to look at all r. In other words, we need to consider higher and higher re-embeddings given by |-rK_X| and all their flat degenerations under one parameter group. This is similar to the asymptotic Chow stability. See for a detailed discussion, especially for the implications among different notions of stability. Nevertheless, the directions which were not addressed in were more subtle. While it is proved in that any polarized manifold (X,L) with a cscK metric and finite automorphism group is asymptotically Chow stable, however, this is known to not hold for either X has an infinite automorphism group (see ) or X is singular (see ).

Consider a smooth Fano variety $X$, such that there is an effective torus action $T(\cong \mathbb{G}_m^r)$ on $X$. Then for any (integral) coweight $\mathbb{G}_m\to T$, we can define a  test configuration $ \mathcal{X}\cong X\times \mathbb{A}^1$ and $\mathcal{L}\cong  -K_{X\times \mathbb{A}^1} $ with the $\mathbb{G}_m$-action given by 
\[
t\cdot (x,a)\to (t(x), t\cdot a).
\]
This kind of test configuration is called {\it a product test configuration}. Since if we reverse the action of $\mathbb{G}_m$, the total weight will change the sign, we conclude that if $X$ is K-semistable, then ${\rm Fut}( \mathcal{X},\mathcal{L})=0$ for all product test configurations. This condition was first introduced in \cite{Fut83}.

nodes.statement: Started from any test configuration X, we will use the the minimal model program to modify X such that at the end we obtain a special test configuration X^s, and during the process the generalized Futaki invariants decrease. The modification consists of a few steps. Step 0: If we replace X by the normalization ncolon X^nto Xtimes_zto z^dA^1, then we have dcdot Fut(X,L )ge Fut(X^n,L^n:=n^*L) with the equality holds if and only if X^ntoXtimes_zto z^dA^1 is an isomorphism outside codimension at least 2. This can be seen by directly applying the intersection formula . After Step 0, we can always assume the special fiber is reduced. The following steps will all involve minimal model program constructions. The main observation is the following calculation: denote by L the polarization on X, such that L|_X_tsim -rK_X_t for tneq 0, so we can write L+rK_X_tsim E which is a divisor supported over 0. Then let t>0 such that L_t=L+tE is still ample, then applying , we have fracddtFut(X,L_t) =fracn2(-K_X)^n(frac1rbarL_t)^n-1cdot (frac1rE)^2le 0\ \ . Step 1: From X^n, we can construct the log canonical modification of f^lccolon X^lcto (X,X^n_0) (see ), where X^n_0 is the special fiber. By a suitable base change, we can assume that the special fiber X^lc_0 of X^lc is also reduced. Let F be the reduced exceptional divisor. Then by the definition of the lc modification, K_X^lc+f^lc_*(X^n_0)+F=K_X^lc+X^lc_0sim K_X^lc is ample over X^n. So E=frac1rf^lc*L^n+K_X^lc is ample over X^n and L^lc_t:=frac1rf^lc*L^n+tE is ample for some 0<tll 1. Therefore, implies Fut(X^lc,L^lc_t)le Fut(X^n,L^n), and the equality holds if and only if (X^n,X^n_0) is log canonical. Step 2: Replacing L^lc by its power, we can assume that H:=L^lc-K_X^lc is ample. Then we run K_X^lc-MMP with the scaling of H (see ), which is automatically G_m-equivariant in each step. Thus we get a sequence of numbers t_0=1>t_1ge t_2ge...ge t_m-1> t_m=frac1r, with a sequence of models \[ X^lc=Y_0dasharrow Y_1dasharrow cdots dasharrow Y_m-1 \] such that if we let H_i be the pushforward of H on Y_i, K_Y_i+sH_i is nef for any sin [t_i-1,t_i]. Moreover, we have K_Y_m-1+t_mH_m-1sim _Q 0. Thus \[ K_Y_m-1+t_m-1H_m-1sim_Q(t_m-1-t_m)H_m-1 \] is big and nef. Let X^an be the ample model of H_m-1 and L^an the ample Q-divisor induced by H_m-1. If we use to define the generalized Futaki invariant when L is a big and nef line Q-bundle, then implies Fut(X^lc,L^lc)&=&Fut(Y_0, K_Y_0+H)\\ &ge &Fut(Y_0, K_Y_0+t_1H_0)\\ &=& Fut(Y_1, K_Y_1+t_1H_1)\\ &ge& cdots\\ &=& Fut(Y_m-1, K_Y_1+t_m-1H_m-1)\\ &=& Fut(X^an, L^an), and the equality holds if and only if X^lc=X^an. We note that since -K_X^an is proportional to L^an, we indeed have Fut(X^an, L^an)=-frac12(n+1)(-K_X)^nleft(K_barX^an/P^1right)^n+1. (In particular, (X^an, L^an) is a weakly special test configuration.) Step 3: In the last step, by a tie-breaking argument, we can show after a possible base change, by running a suitable minimal model program, we can construct a model such that (X^s, X^s_0) is plt and the discrepancy of X^s_0 with respect to (X^an,X_0^an) is -1. By an intersection number calculation, we have -frac12(n+1)(-K_X)^nleft(K_barX^an/P^1right)^n+1ge -frac12(n+1)(-K_X)^nleft(K_barX^s/P^1right)^n+1 and the equality holds if and only if X^an=X^s.

Started from any test configuration ${\mathcal{X}}$, we will use the the minimal model program to modify ${\mathcal{X}}$ such that at the end we obtain a special test configuration ${\mathcal{X}}^{\rm s}$, and during the process the generalized Futaki invariants decrease. The modification consists of a few steps.

\noindent {\it Step 0:} If we replace ${\mathcal{X}}$ by the normalization $n\colon {\mathcal{X}}^n\to {\mathcal{X}}\times_{z\to z^d}\mathbb{A}^1$, then we have 
$$d\cdot {\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}},{\mathcal{L}} )\ge {\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}}^n,{\mathcal{L}}^n:=n^*{\mathcal{L}})$$ with the equality holds if and only if ${\mathcal{X}}^n\to{\mathcal{X}}\times_{z\to z^d}\mathbb{A}^1$ is an isomorphism outside codimension at least 2. This can be seen by directly applying the intersection formula \eqref{e-inter}.

\begin{keyidea}After Step 0, we can always assume the special fiber is reduced. The following steps will all involve minimal model program constructions. The main observation is the following calculation: denote by ${\mathcal{L}}$ the polarization on ${\mathcal{X}}$, such that ${\mathcal{L}}|_{X_t}\sim -rK_{X_t}$ for $t\neq 0$, so we can write ${\mathcal{L}}+rK_{X_t}\sim E$ which is a divisor supported over $0$. Then let $t>0$ such that ${\mathcal{L}}_t={\mathcal{L}}+tE$ is still ample, then applying \eqref{e-inter}, we have
\begin{eqnarray}\label{e-decreasing}
\frac{d}{dt}{\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}},{\mathcal{L}}_t) =\frac{n}{2(-K_X)^n}(\frac{1}{r}\bar{{\mathcal{L}}}_t)^{n-1}\cdot (\frac{1}{r}E)^2\le 0\ \ .
\end{eqnarray}
\end{keyidea}

\noindent {\it Step 1:} From ${\mathcal{X}}^n$, we can construct the log canonical modification of $f^{\rm lc}\colon {\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}\to ({\mathcal{X}},X^n_0)$ (see \cite[Theorem 1.32]{Kol13}), where $X^n_0$ is the special fiber. By a suitable base change, we can assume that the special fiber $X^{\rm lc}_0$ of ${\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}$ is also reduced. Let $F$ be the reduced exceptional divisor. Then by the definition of the lc modification, 
$$K_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}}+f^{\rm lc}_*(X^n_0)+F=K_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}}+X^{\rm lc}_0\sim K_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}}$$
 is ample over ${\mathcal{X}}^n$.   So $E=\frac{1}{r}f^{{\rm lc}*}{\mathcal{L}}^n+K_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc }}$ is ample over $X^n$ and ${\mathcal{L}}^{\rm lc}_t:=\frac{1}{r}f^{{\rm lc}*}{\mathcal{L}}^n+tE$ is ample  for some $0<t\ll 1$. Therefore, \eqref{e-decreasing} implies
$ {\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc},{\mathcal{L}}^{\rm lc}_t)\le {\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}}^n,{\mathcal{L}}^n),$
and the equality holds if and only if $({\mathcal{X}}^n,X^n_0)$ is log canonical. 

\medskip

\noindent {\it Step 2:} Replacing ${\mathcal{L}}^{\rm lc}$ by its power, we can assume that $H:={\mathcal{L}}^{lc}-K_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}}$ is ample. Then we run $K_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}}$-MMP with the scaling of $H$ (see \cite{BCHM10}), which is automatically $\mathbb{G}_m$-equivariant in each step. Thus we get a sequence of numbers $t_0=1>t_1\ge t_2\ge...\ge t_{m-1}> t_m=\frac{1}{r}$, with a sequence of models
\[
{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}=Y_0\dasharrow Y_1\dasharrow \cdots \dasharrow Y_{m-1}
\]
such that if we let $H_i$ be the pushforward of $H$ on $Y_i$, $K_{Y_i}+sH_i$ is nef for any $s\in [t_{i-1},t_i]$. Moreover, we have $K_{Y_{m-1}}+t_mH_{m-1}\sim _{\mathbb{Q}} 0$. Thus 
\[
K_{Y_{m-1}}+t_{m-1}H_{m-1}\sim_{\mathbb{Q}}(t_{m-1}-t_m)H_{m-1}
\]
is big and nef. Let $X^{\rm an}$ be the ample model of $H_{m-1}$ and ${\mathcal{L}}^{\rm an}$ the ample $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor induced by $H_{m-1}$. If we use \eqref{e-inter} to define the generalized Futaki invariant  when ${\mathcal{L}}$ is a big and nef line $\mathbb{Q}$-bundle, then \eqref{e-decreasing} implies 
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc},{\mathcal{L}}^{\rm lc})&=&{\rm Fut}(Y_0, K_{Y_0}+H)\\
&\ge &{\rm Fut}(Y_0, K_{Y_0}+t_1H_0)\\
&=& {\rm Fut}(Y_1, K_{Y_1}+t_1H_1)\\
&\ge& \cdots\\
&=& {\rm Fut}(Y_{m-1}, K_{Y_1}+t_{m-1}H_{m-1})\\
&=& {\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}}^{\rm an}, {\mathcal{L}}^{\rm an}),
\end{eqnarray*}
 and the equality holds if and only if ${\mathcal{X}}^{\rm lc}={\mathcal{X}}^{\rm an}$. We note that since $-K_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm an}}$ is proportional to ${\mathcal{L}}^{\rm an}$, we indeed have 
 \begin{eqnarray}\label{e-anti}
  {\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}}^{\rm an}, {\mathcal{L}}^{\rm an})=-\frac{1}{2(n+1)(-K_X)^n}\left(K_{\bar{{\mathcal{X}}}^{\rm an}/\mathbb{P}^1}\right)^{n+1}.
\end{eqnarray}
\medskip
(In particular, $({\mathcal{X}}^{\rm an}, {\mathcal{L}}^{\rm an})$ is a weakly special test configuration.)

\noindent {\it Step 3:} In the last step, by a tie-breaking argument, we can show after a possible base change, by running a suitable minimal model program, we can construct a model such that $({\mathcal{X}}^{\rm s}, X^{\rm s}_0)$ is plt and the discrepancy of $X^{\rm s}_0$ with respect to $({\mathcal{X}}^{\rm an},X_0^{\rm an})$ is $-1$. By an intersection number calculation, we have 
$$ -\frac{1}{2(n+1)(-K_X)^n}\left(K_{\bar{{\mathcal{X}}}^{\rm an}/\mathbb{P}^1}\right)^{n+1}\ge -\frac{1}{2(n+1)(-K_X)^n}\left(K_{\bar{{\mathcal{X}}}^{\rm s}/\mathbb{P}^1}\right)^{n+1}$$
and the equality holds if and only if ${\mathcal{X}}^{\rm an}={\mathcal{X}}^{\rm s}.$

Since ${\rm tr. deg}(K({\mathcal{X}})/K(X))=1$, by Abhyankar's inequality, we know that

Consider a section $s\in H^0(-mK_X)$ for $m$ sufficiently divisible. Let $D_s$ be the closure of $(s)\times \mathbb{A}^1$ on $X\times \mathbb{A}^1$. Fix a common log resolution $\widehat{{\mathcal{X}}}$ of ${\mathcal{X}}$ and $X\times \mathbb{A}^1$ 
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
  & \widehat{{\mathcal{X}}}  \arrow[dr, "\psi'"] \arrow[dl,swap,"\psi"]& \\
 X\times \mathbb{A}^1  \arrow[rr, dashrightarrow, "\phi'"] & & {\mathcal{X}}.
   \end{tikzcd} 
    \end{center}
Denote by $X_0$ the special fiber of ${\mathcal{X}}$.     So 
\begin{eqnarray}\label{e-weight}
\psi^*(D_s)=\widehat{D_s}+({\rm ord}_{X_0}(\bar{s}))\widetilde{X_0}+E\in H^0(	-mK_{\widehat{{\mathcal{X}}}}+m\cdot a(X_0,X\times \mathbb{A}^1)\widetilde{X}_0+F) 
\end{eqnarray} where $\widehat{D}_{s}$ and $\widetilde{X_0}$ are the birational transforms of $D_{s}$ and $X_0$ on $\widehat{{\mathcal{X}}}$ and ${\rm Supp}(E)$ as well as ${\rm Supp}(F)$ supporting over $0$ do not contain the birational transform of $X\times\{0\}$ and $X_0$. We know 
$$a(X_0,X\times \mathbb{A}^1)=A(X_0,X\times \mathbb{A}^1)-1=c\cdot A_{X}(E ) \mbox{\ \ and \ \ }{\rm ord}_{X_0}(\bar{s})=c\cdot {\rm ord}_E(s),$$
so if we denote by $D_s'=\psi'_*\big(\widehat{D_s})$, pushforward \eqref{e-weight} under $\psi'$, it becomes 
$$D_s'+(c\cdot{\rm ord}_E(s))X_0\in H^0(-mK_{{\mathcal{X}}}+mc\cdot A_X(E){X}_0).$$
 We choose  a basis $\{s_1,..., s_{N_m}\}$ $(N_m=\dim H^0(-mK_X))$ of $H^0(-mK_{X})$ which is compatible with the filtration, that is, if we let $j_i=\dim \mathcal{F}^i(H^0(-mK_X))$, then 
$\{s_1,..., s_{j_i}\}$ form a basis of $\mathcal{F}^i(H^0(-mK_X))$. The above computation says
the total weight $w_m$ of $\mathbb{G}_m$ on $H^0(-mK_{{\mathcal{X}}})$ is
\[
 w_m=\sum_ic\cdot(j_{i}-j_{i+1})i-rmc,
\]
and if we divide by $\frac{m^{n+1}}{n!}$ and let $m\to \infty$, we have 
\[
\lim_{m\to \infty}\frac{w_m}{m^{n+1}/n!}=c\cdot \int^{\infty}_{0}{\rm vol}(-K_X-t\cdot E)dt-cA_X(E)(-K_X)^n=-c(-K_X)^n\beta_X(E),
\]
where we use
\[
\lim_m \frac{1}{m^{n+1} /n!}\sum_i(j_{i}-j_{i+1})i=\lim_m \frac{1}{m^{n+1} /n!}\sum_ij_i=\int^{\infty}_{0}{\rm vol}(-K_X-t\cdot E)dt 
\]
by the dominated convergence theorem. 

On the other hand, a simple Riemann-Roch calculation implies 
$$\lim_{m\to \infty}\frac{w_m}{m^{n+1}/n!}=\frac{1}{n+1}(-K_{\bar{{\mathcal{X}}}/\mathbb{P}^1})^{n+1}=-2(-K_X)^n\cdot {\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}})$$ by \eqref{e-anti}.

\label{e-bounded} 
One of the first striking consequences of the valuative criterion Theorem \ref{t-valkstable} is the following statement proved by Fujita in \cite{Fuj18}: The volume of an $n$-dimensional K-semistable $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano variety is at most $(n+1)^n$. 

Let $X$ be a K-semistable $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano variety. Pick up a smooth point $x\in X$, and blow up $x$, we get $\mu\colon Y\to X$ with an exceptional divisor $E$. 
Since 
\[
0\to {\mathfrak{m}}_x^k\otimes \mathcal{O}_X(-mK_X)\to \mathcal{O}_X(-mK_X) \to  \mathcal{O}_X(-mK_X)\otimes (\mathcal{O}_X/ {\mathfrak{m}}_x^k)\to 0,
\]
we know that 
$$h^0(\mathcal{O}_Y(\mu^*(-mK_X)-kE))\ge h^0(\mathcal{O}_X(-mK_X))-h^0(\mathcal{O}_X(-mK_X)\otimes (\mathcal{O}_X/ {\mathfrak{m}}_x^k).$$
Thus we have
\begin{eqnarray*}
0\le (-K_X)^n\cdot\beta(E)&=&n\cdot (-K_X)^n-\int^{\infty}_{0}{\rm vol}(\mu^*(-K_X)-tE)dt\\
&\le &n\cdot (-K_X)^n-\int^{((-K_X)^n)^{\frac1n}}_{0}((-K_X)^n-t^n),
\end{eqnarray*}
which immediately implies $(-K_X)^n\le (n+1)^n. $

If $X$ is singular, and we choose $x$ to be a singularity, then an even stronger restriction on the volume in terms of the local volume of the singularity  is obtained in \cite{Liu18}. See Theorem \ref{t-localtoglobal}.

nodes.statement: It turns out that the invariant delta(X) also has an older origin from the differential geometry in terms of twisted K\"ahler-Einstein metrics: For a Fano manifold X, in and then in , an invariant called the greatest Ricci lower bound of X was first defined and studied as \[ small sup\t in [0, 1]\ | mbox a K\"ahler metric omega in c_1(X) mbox such that Ric(omega) > tomega\. \] Later this invariant was further studied in etc. It is shown in that for a Fano manifold X, the greatest Ricci lower bound is equal to min\1, delta(X)\.
nodes.raw_latex:
It turns out that the invariant $\delta(X)$ also has an older origin from the differential geometry in terms of twisted K\"ahler-Einstein metrics:
For a Fano manifold $X$, in \cite{Tia92} and then in \cite{Rub08, Rub09}, an invariant called {\it the greatest Ricci lower bound } of $X$ was first defined and studied  as
\[
\small{
\sup\{t \in [0, 1]\  | \mbox{ a K\"ahler metric } \omega \in c_1(X) \mbox{ such that } {\rm Ric}(\omega) > t\omega\}. 
}
\]

Later this invariant was  further studied  in \cite{Sze11, Li11, SW16} etc.
It is shown in \cite{BBJ15, CRZ18}  that for a Fano manifold $X$,  the greatest Ricci lower bound is equal to $\min\{1, \delta(X)\}$.

nodes.name: Yau-Tian-Donaldson Conjecture
nodes.statement: Consider the case delta(X)=1. In this case, Conjecture says that a Fano variety is K-stable if and only if it is uniformly K-stable. We can also formulate an equivariant version of the conjecture which predicts that a Fano variety K-polystable if and only if it is reduced uniformly K-stable (see Definition ). It has been proved recently that any reduced uniformly K-stable Fano variety has a K\"ahler-Einstein metric (). Therefore Conjecture (resp. its equivariant version Conjecture ) predicts that any K-stable (resp. K-polystable) Q-Fano variety admits a K\"ahler-Einstein metric, hence provide a new proof of Yau-Tian-Donaldson Conjecture which would work even for singular Fano varieties.

\label{r-YTDnew}
Consider the case $\delta(X)=1$. In this case, Conjecture \ref{c-maxidd} says that a Fano variety is K-stable if and only if it is uniformly K-stable. We can also formulate an equivariant version of the conjecture which predicts that a Fano variety K-polystable if and only if it is reduced uniformly K-stable (see Definition \ref{d-reduceduniform}). nodes.name: Quasi-monomial valuations
nodes.statement: Denote Zto X a log resolution with simple normal crossing divisors E_1,...., E_r on Z. Denote by alpha=(alpha_1,...., alpha_r)in R^r_ge 0. Assume bigcap^r_i=1 E_ineq emptyset; and there exists a component Csubset cap E_i, such that around the generic point eta of C, E_i is given by the equation z_i in O_Z,eta(C). We define a valuation v_alpha to be v_alpha(f)=min \sum alpha_ibeta_i|\ c_beta(eta)neq 0\, and all such valuations are called quasi-monomial valuations. It is precisely the valuations satisfying the equality case in Abhyankar's inequality, therefore, it is another description of Abhyankar valuation. We call the dimension of the Q-vector space spanned by \alpha_1,...., alpha_r\ the rational rank of v_alpha, and one can show v_alpha is a rescaling of a divisorial valuation if and only if r=1. For fixed Csubset (Z,E) as above, the valuations v_alpha for all alpha gives a simplicial cone which is a natural subspace in Val_X.

\label{e-quasi} Denote $Z\to X$ a log resolution with simple normal crossing divisors $E_1$,...., $E_r$ on $Z$. Denote by $\alpha=(\alpha_1$,...., $\alpha_r)\in \mathbb{R}^r_{\ge 0}$. Assume $\bigcap^r_{i=1} E_i\neq \emptyset$; and there exists a component $C\subset \cap E_i$, such that around the generic point $\eta$ of $C$, $E_i$ is given by the equation $z_i$ in $\mathcal{O}_{Z,\eta(C)}$.
We define a valuation $v_{\alpha}$ to be
$$v_{\alpha}(f)=\min \{\sum \alpha_i\beta_i|\ c_{\beta}(\eta)\neq 0\},$$
and all such valuations are called {\it quasi-monomial valuations}. It is precisely the valuations satisfying the equality case in Abhyankar's inequality, therefore, it is another description of Abhyankar valuation. 

We call the dimension of the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space spanned by $\{\alpha_1$,...., $\alpha_r\}$ the rational rank of $v_{\alpha}$, and one can show $v_{\alpha}$ is a rescaling of a divisorial valuation if and only if $r=1$. By \eqref{e-delta}, we can pick a sufficiently large $m$, such that
$$\delta_m(X)\le (1+\epsilon)\delta(X)\le (1+\epsilon)^2\delta_m(X).$$  
We may also assume $S_m(E)\le (1+\epsilon) S(E)$ for any divisor $E$ by Proposition \ref{p-Sapproximation}(2). There exists  an $m$-basis type ${\mathbb{Q}}$-divisor $D_m$ and a divisor $E$ over $X$ with
$$\delta_m(X)={\rm lct}(X; D_m)=\frac{A(E)}{{\rm ord}_E(D_m)}=\frac{A(E)}{S_m(E)}.$$

We first assume $\delta(X)<1$. So we can also assume $\delta_m(X)<1$. Thus we can find a general ${\mathbb{Q}}$-divisor $H\sim_{{\mathbb{Q}}} -(1-\delta_m)K_X$, such that $(X, \delta_m D_m+H)$ is log canonical, and $E$ is an lc place of such divisor. Thus
$$\delta(E)=\frac{A(E)}{S(E)}\le (1+\epsilon)\frac{A(E)}{S_m(E)}\le (1+\epsilon)^2\delta(X).$$
Then we can pick a sequence $\epsilon\to 0$ and a corresponding sequence of $E$. 

\medskip

When $\delta(X)=1$, we need some extra perturbation argument. Consider the pseudo-effective threshold 
\[
\mbox{$T(E):=\sup\{ t\ |-\mu^*K_X-tE \mbox{ is pseudo-effective} \}$}
\]
Then by \cite{Fuj19c}*{Proposition 2.1}, we know 
$T(E)\ge \frac{n+1}{n}S(E)$ for any $E$. Thus we can find a divisor $D\sim_{\mathbb{Q}} -K_X$, such that 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
{\rm mult}_E(D)&\ge(1+\frac{1}{n}-\epsilon_0)S(E)\ge (1+\frac{1}{n}-\epsilon_0)\frac{S(E)}{S_m(E)}S_m(E) \\ 
&\ge (1+\frac{1}{n}-\epsilon_0)\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\frac{A(E)}{\delta_m} \ge (1+\frac{1}{2n})A(E),
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
if we choose $\epsilon_0, \epsilon$ sufficiently small.


Fix $t\in (0, \alpha(X))$, then the pair $(X,t D)$ is klt, and 
$$A_{X,t D}(E)=A_X(E)-t\cdot  {\rm mult}_E(D)  \qquad \mbox{and} \qquad  S_{X,tD}=(1-t)S(E),$$
which implies that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\delta(X,t D)&\le\frac{A_{X,t D}(E)}{S_{X,t D}(E)}\le  \frac{1-t(1+\frac{1}{2n})}{1-t}\delta(E) \\
&\le\frac{(1-t(1+\frac{1}{2n}))(1+\epsilon)}{1-t} \delta_m<1,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
if we choose $\epsilon$ sufficiently small (depending on $t$).

Thus for any such $t$, by the case of $\delta(X,tD)<1$, we know that there exists an lc place $F$ of $(X,tD+D')$ for a ${\mathbb{Q}}$-complement $D'$ with $\delta_{X,tD}(F)$ sufficiently close to $\delta(X,t D)$.
On the other hand, since $\alpha(X)\le {\rm lct}(X,D)\le  \frac{A_X(F)}{{\rm mult}_F(D)}$, 
$$A_{X,tD}(F)=A(F)-t\cdot {\rm mult}_FD\ge (1-\frac{t}{\alpha(X)})A(F),$$ 
which implies that
$$\delta(F)=\frac{A(F)}{S(F)}\le \frac{(1-t)A_{X,tD}(F)}{(1-\frac{t}{\alpha(X)})S_{X,tD}(F)}=\frac{1-t}{1-\frac{t}{\alpha(X)}}\delta_{X,tD}(F). $$
Since $\delta(X,tD)\le \frac{1}{1-t}$,  we can choose a sequence $t_m\to 0$ and a corresponding sequence of lc places $F_m$ with $\lim \delta(F_m)\to 1$.

nodes.statement: For a Z -value divisorial valuation vin Val_X over an n-dimensional Q-Fano variety X, it arises from a nontrivial weakly special test configuration with a irreducible central fiber if and only if there exists an Q-complement D of X such that v is an lc place of X. conclusions: For a Z -value divisorial valuation vin Val_X over an n-dimensional Q-Fano variety X, it arises from a nontrivial weakly special test configuration with a irreducible central fiber if and only if there exists an Q-complement D of X such that v is an lc place of X.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{t-weakspecial}
For a ${\mathbb{Z} }$-value divisorial valuation $v\in {\rm Val}_X$ over an $n$-dimensional ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Fano variety $X$, it  arises from a nontrivial weakly special test configuration with a irreducible central fiber if and only if there exists an $\mathbb{Q}$-complement $D$ of $X$ such that $v$ is an lc place of $X$. In other words, a divisorial valuation is weakly special if and only if it is an lc place of an $\mathbb{Q}$-complement.

nodes.statement: In Proposition , we have seen from an lc place E of a mathbb Q-complement D, we can obtain a weakly special test configuration. Then if we consider a valuation v=acdot ord_E for an lc place E of a Q-complement and ain mathbb N_+, then in the proof of Proposition , we take the weighted blowup of E_A^1 and Xtimes\0\ with weight (1,a), and run an MMP as before, we obtain a weakly special test configuration as desired. Conversely, from a weakly special test configuration X with an irreducible central fiber, we want to prove the induced Z -valuation v is an lc place of a Q-complement D. The original proof in used the cone construction. Here we gave a (simpler) global argumentfootnoteIt is suggested by Harold Blum., relying on some latter results in Section . Let ord_E be the induced divisorial valuation by the weakly special test configuration. Consider the valuation of ord_E on R:=bigoplus_min N H^0(-mrK_X). Then we know A(E)-S(E)=beta(E)ge beta(F_E)=fracmu_1(F_E)-S(F_E)rge D^NA(F_E)=A(E)-S(E). See Definition for the invariants of F_E; the inequalities follow from Proposition ; and the last equality follows from the fact that X is weakly special test configuration. This implies that rA(E)=mu_1(F_E) as rS(E)=S(F_E). The rest follows from which we will include here for reader's convenience. Let I_m,p(F):=Im left( F^p R_m otimes O_X(-rmK_X) to O_Xright) and I^(t)_bullet=(I_m,mt). The function tmapsto lct(X;I^(t)_bullet) is piecewise linear on (0,rT_X(E)] due to the finite generation assumption. Then \[ lct(X,;I^(rcdot A_X(E))_bullet)le fracA_X(E)ord_E(I^(rcdot A_X(E))_bullet)le fracA_X(E)rcdot A_X(E) = frac1r, \] thus lct(X;I^(rcdot A_X(E))_bullet) = frac1r. Since gr_F_ER is finitely generated, then \[ lct(X;I^ (rcdot A_X(E))_bullet)=mcdot lct(X;I_m, mrA_X(E)))= frac1r. \] for some sufficiently divisible m. This means there is a divisor Din |-mrK_X| with ord_E(D)ge mrA_X(E) and (X,frac1mrD) is log canonical. Thus E is an lc place of (X,frac1mrD).

In Proposition \ref{p-lctotest}, we have seen from an lc place $E$ of a $\mathbb Q$-complement $D$, we can obtain a weakly special test configuration.
Then if we consider a valuation $v=a\cdot {\rm ord}_E$ for an lc place $E$ of a $\mathbb{Q}$-complement and $a\in \mathbb N_+$, then in the proof of Proposition \ref{p-lctotest}, we take the weighted blowup of $E_{\mathbb{A}^1}$ and $X\times\{0\}$ with weight $(1,a)$, and run an MMP as before, we obtain a weakly special test configuration as desired. 



\smallskip

Conversely, from a weakly special test configuration ${\mathcal{X}}$ with an irreducible central fiber, we want to prove the induced ${\mathbb{Z} }$-valuation $v$ is an lc place of a ${\mathbb{Q}}$-complement $D$. The original proof in \cite{BLX19} used the cone construction. Here we gave a (simpler) global argument\footnote{It is suggested by Harold Blum.}, relying on some latter results in Section \ref{s-Ding}.

Let ${\rm ord}_E$ be the induced divisorial valuation by the weakly special test configuration.  Consider the valuation of ${\rm ord}_E$ on $R:=\bigoplus_{m\in {\mathbb{N} }}H^0(-mrK_X)$. Then we know 
$$A(E)-S(E)=\beta(E)\ge \beta(\mathcal{F}_E)=\frac{\mu_1(\mathcal{F}_{E})-S(\mathcal{F}_E)}{r}\ge \mathbf{D}^{\mathrm{NA}}(\mathcal{F}_E)=A(E)-S(E).$$
See Definition \ref{d-filbeta} for the invariants of $\mathcal{F}_E$; the inequalities follow from Proposition \ref{l-betading};
and the last equality follows from the fact that ${\mathcal{X}}$ is weakly special test configuration. This implies that $rA(E)=\mu_1({\mathcal{F}_{E}})$ as $rS(E)=S(\mathcal{F}_E)$. The rest follows from \cite[Theorem A.7]{XZ19} which we will include here for reader's convenience.

Let $I_{m,p}(\mathcal{F}):={\rm Im} \left(  \mathcal{F}^p R_m \otimes {\mathcal{O}}_{X}(-rmK_X) \to {\mathcal{O}}_X\right)$ and $I^{(t)}_{\bullet}=(I_{m,mt})$. The function $t\mapsto {\rm lct}(X;I^{(t)}_\bullet)$ is  piecewise linear  on $(0,rT_{X}(E)]$ due to the finite generation assumption.
Then
\[
{\rm lct}(X,;I^{(r\cdot A_{X}(E))}_\bullet)\le \frac{A_{X}(E)}{{\rm ord}_E(I^{(r\cdot A_{X}(E))}_\bullet)}\le \frac{A_{X}(E)}{r\cdot A_{X}(E)} = \frac{1}{r},
\]
thus ${\rm lct}(X;I^{(r\cdot A_{X}(E))}_\bullet) = \frac{1}{r}$.
Since ${\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}_E}R$ is finitely generated, then
\[
{\rm lct}(X;I^{ (r\cdot A_{X}(E))}_\bullet)=m\cdot {\rm lct}(X;I_{m, mrA_{X}(E))})= \frac{1}{r}.
\]
for some sufficiently divisible $m$. This means there is a divisor $D\in |-mrK_X|$ with ${\rm ord}_E(D)\ge mrA_{X}(E)$ and $(X,\frac{1}{mr}D)$ is log canonical. Thus $E$ is an lc place of $(X,\frac{1}{mr}D)$.

nodes.raw_latex:
We first prove $(1)\Longleftrightarrow (2)$. A test configuration ${\mathcal{X}}$ is special if and only if for any effective $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor $D\sim_{\mathbb Q}-K_X$, there exists a positive $\epsilon$, such that $({\mathcal{X}}, \epsilon{\mathcal{D}})$ is a weakly special test configuration where ${\mathcal{D}}$ is the closure of $D\times \mathbb{G}_m$ in ${\mathcal{X}}$. This is equivalent to saying that for $D$, there are a positive $\epsilon$ and  an effective $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor $D'\sim_{\mathbb{Q}}-K_X$ of $X$ such that $E$ is an lc place of  the lc pair $(X,\epsilon D+(1-\epsilon)D')$.

Now we assume $E$ satisfies the conditions in (2). Then we have $\mathbb{Q}$-divisors $D'\sim_{\mathbb Q}D''\sim_{\mathbb Q}-K_X$ such that $A_{X,D'}(E)>0$ and $A_{X,D''}(E)<0$. By choosing one of them as $D_1$ and an appropriate $a\in [0,1)$, we have $A_{X,aD_1+(1-a)D}(E)=0$. 
Thus for a sufficiently small $\epsilon$, $\Big(X,\epsilon\big((1-a)D_1+aD\big)+(1-\epsilon)D^*)\Big)$ is lc and has $E$ as its lc place. 


Conversely, if we take $D$ to be a general $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor whose support does not contain ${\rm Cent}_X(E)$, then since for some $\epsilon>0$, $E$ is an lc place of $(X, \epsilon D+(1-\epsilon)D')$ from our assumption, we have 
$$A_X(E)=A_{X,\epsilon D}(E)\le T_{X,\epsilon D}(E)=(1-\epsilon)T_X(E).$$ 
To see the second property, we denote by $\mu\colon Y\to X$ the model precisely extracting $E$.  Then we run MMP for $-K_Y-E$ to get a model $Y'$, and we claim $(Y',E')$ is plt. Otherwise, we can find an effective ${\mathbb{Q}}$-divisor $D_{Y'}\sim_{\mathbb{Q}}-K_{Y'}-E'$ such that $(Y', E'+ \epsilon D_{Y'})$ is not log canonical for any $\epsilon>0$, as $-K_{Y'}-E'$ is big. This yields an effective $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor $D\sim_{\mathbb{Q}}-K_X$ on $X$ violating our assumption on $E$. Now we pick up a general ${\mathbb{Q}}$-complement of $(Y', E')$, it induces a ${\mathbb{Q}}$-complement $D^*$ with $E$ the only lc place of $(X,D^*)$.  

Finally, from the above discussions, one can easily see $(1)\Longrightarrow (3)\Longrightarrow (2)$. We leave the details to the reader.

The \emph{normalized volume function} $$\widehat{\rm vol}_{Y,x}:{\rm Val}_{Y,x}\to(0, +\infty]$$

  \[

            +\infty & \textrm{ if }A_{Y}(v)=+\infty.
           \end{cases}
 \]
 The \emph{volume of the singularity} $x\in Y$ is defined as
 \[
  \widehat{\rm vol}(x, Y):=\inf_{v\in{\rm Val}_{Y,x}}\widehat{\rm vol}_{Y,x}(v).
 \]
 The previous infimum is a minimum by the main result in \cite{Blu18} (see also \cite[Remark 3.8]{Xu19}).

Let $x\in Y$ be a klt singularity. 
We recall that a prime divisor $E$ over a klt point $x\in Y$ is called a {\it Koll\'ar component} (resp. {\it weak Koll\'ar component}) if there is a birational morphism $\mu\colon Y'\to Y$ isomorphic over $X\setminus\{x\}$, such that $E={\rm Ex}(\mu)$, $(Y',E)$ is plt (resp. log canonical) and $-K_{Y'}-E$ is ample over $Y$. These notions can be considered as a local birational version of special degenerations (resp. weakly special degenerations with irreducible fibers).

Let ${\mathfrak{a}}_{t,p}:={\mathfrak{a}}_p(v_t)$. So ${\mathfrak{a}}_{t,p}$ contains $ \oplus_{m\geq p} R_m$. We claim the following hold:
\begin{eqnarray}\label{e-volume}
\mbox{ ${\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}}_{t,\bullet}) =  r^n (-K_X)^n - (n+1) \int_{0}^{\infty} {\rm vol} (\mathcal{F}_E R^{(x)}) \frac{ t\, dx}{(1+tx)^{n+2}}$}.
\end{eqnarray}


This follows from the argument in \cite[(18)-(25)]{Li17}. For the reader's convenience, we give a brief proof.
For $t\in {\mathbb{R}}_{>0 }$, we have 
\begin{align*}
{\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}}_{t,\bullet })&=\lim_{p\to \infty}  \frac{(n+1)!}{p^{n+1}}\dim_k (R/{\mathfrak{a}}_{t,p})\\
&=\lim_{p\to \infty}  \frac{(n+1)!}{p^{n+1}}\sum^{\infty}_{m=0}\dim_k  (R_m/ \mathcal{F}_E^{{(p-m)}/{t}} R_m ) \\
&=\lim_{p\to \infty}  \frac{(n+1)!}{p^{n+1}}\sum^{p}_{m=0}\left(\dim_k R_m - \dim_k  \mathcal{F}_E^{{(p-m)}/{t}} R_m \right)\\
& = {\rm vol}(L)  - \lim_{p\to \infty}  \frac{(n+1)!}{p^{n+1}} \sum_{m=0}^p \dim_k \mathcal{F}_E^{{(p-m)}/{t}} R_m .
\end{align*}
Then we can identify the limit of the summation with the integral in \eqref{e-volume}, where a change of the variable is needed (see \cite[(25)]{Li17}, where  one chooses $c_1=0$, $\alpha=\beta=\frac{1}{t}$). 

Computing the derivative, we have 
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\widehat{\rm vol}(v_t) \Bigr \rvert_{t=0^+} =a(n+1)\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^n{\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}}_{0,\bullet} )+ \frac{1}{r^{n+1}} \frac{d}{dt} \left({\rm mult} ({\mathfrak{a}}_{t, \bullet} )\right)\Bigr\rvert_{t=0^+}.$$
From \eqref{e-volume}, we know ${\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}}_{0,\bullet})=r^n(-K_X-\Delta)^n$
and
\begin{align*}
 \frac{d}{dt} \left( {\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}}_{t,\bullet} ) \right) \Bigr\rvert_{t=0^+}&=-
 (n+1)\int_0^\infty   \left( {\rm vol}(\mathcal{F}_E R^{(x)})\left( \frac{ 1-tx(n+1)}{(1+tx)^{n+3} } \right) \right) \Bigr\rvert_{t=0^+}dx
.  \end{align*}
Since the latter simplifies to $-(n+1)\int^{\infty}_{0} {\rm vol} (\mathcal{F}_E R^{(x)})dx$, thus
\[
\frac{d}{dt} \left( {\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}}_{t,\bullet} ) \right) \Bigr\rvert_{t=0^+}=(n+1)\beta_X(E).
\]

By \cite[Theorem 7]{Liu18}, we know that 
\begin{eqnarray}\label{e-liu}
\widehat{\rm vol}(x,Y)=\inf_{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}})\cdot{\rm lct}(Y,{\mathfrak{a}})^n,
\end{eqnarray}
where the right hand side runs through all ${\mathfrak{m}}_x$-primary ideals. For any ${\mathfrak{a}}$, if we consider the initial degeneration ${\mathfrak{b}}_k$ of ${\mathfrak{a}}^k$, then ${\mathfrak{b}}_{\bullet}$ forms an ideal sequence, and ${\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}})={\rm mult}({\mathfrak{b}}_{\bullet})=\lim\frac{{\rm mult}({\mathfrak{b}}_k)}{k^n}$, and ${\rm lct}(Y;{\mathfrak{a}})\ge \frac{1}{k}{\rm lct}(Y;{\mathfrak{b}}_k)$. Therefore,
$$ {\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}})\cdot{\rm lct}(Y,{\mathfrak{a}})\le \inf_k  {\rm mult}({\mathfrak{b}}_k)\cdot{\rm lct}^n(Y,{\mathfrak{b}}_k) .$$
Therefore, we can restrict the right hand side of \eqref{e-liu} by only running through all $\mathbb{G}_m$-equivariant ${\mathfrak{m}}_x$-primary ideals. 

Started from any $\mathbb{G}_m$-equivariant ${\mathfrak{m}}_x$-primary ideal ${\mathfrak{a}}$, let $c={\rm lct}(Y;{\mathfrak{a}})$. Let $Y'\to Y$ be a dlt modification of $(X,c\cdot {\mathfrak{a}})$ with reduced exceptional divisor $\Gamma$. We can mimic the last step in the proof of Theorem \ref{t-specialdegeneration}, to show that there is a $\mathbb{G}_m$-equivariant Koll\'ar component $E$ (with the model $Y_E\to Y$), such that $a(E, X, c\cdot{\mathfrak{a}})=-1$,
and 
\[
\widehat{\rm vol}(E)=((-K_{Y_E}-E)|_E)^{n-1}\le ((-K_{Y'}-\Gamma)|_\Gamma)^{n-1}\le {\rm mult}({\mathfrak{a}})\cdot{\rm lct}(Y,{\mathfrak{a}})^n.
\]
(see \cite[Section 3.1]{LX20}).

Assume $X$ is K-semistable. To show $v_0={\rm ord}_{X_{\infty}}$ is a minimizer of $\widehat{\rm vol}_{Y,x}$, by Proposition \ref{p-kollar}, it suffices to show that for any Koll\'ar component $E$ over $x\in Y$, we have $\widehat{\rm vol}(E)\ge \widehat{\rm vol}(v_0).$ By Proposition \ref{p-corresp}, we know that $E$ will induces a ray $v_t$ containing $a\cdot {\rm ord}_E$ for some $a\in \mathbb{Q}$, which corresponds to a special test configuration ${\mathcal{X}}$. We can rescale $t$ such that $v_t$ is defined to be the quasimonomial valuation with weights $(1,t)$ along $X_\infty$ and $c\cdot E_{\infty}$, where $c\cdot E_{\infty}$ is the pull back of the divisorial valuation induced by ${\mathcal{X}}$ (see Lemma \ref{l-induced}). 
 
Since $X$ is K-semistable, by Lemma \ref{l-beta=w} and \ref{l-dervolume}, we know that 
$$\frac{d}{dt}\widehat{\rm vol}{(v_t)}|_{t=0}= (n+1)\cdot {\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}})\ge 0.$$
Since $\widehat{\rm vol}(v_t)$ is a convex function on $t$ by \eqref{e-volume} (or see \cite[Section 3.2]{LX18}),
\[\widehat{\rm vol}({\rm ord}_E)=\widehat{\rm vol}(a\cdot {\rm ord}_E)\ge \widehat{\rm vol}(v_0).
\]

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{r-futakifiltration}
The conceptual reason that Lemma \ref{l-dingapproximation} holds is that in the definition of ${\rm Ding}$-invariants, only the leading term of the asymptotic formula is needed. As a comparison, for generalized Futaki invariants one also has to consider the second term. In \cite{Nys12}, the viewpoint of filtrations was taken to study test configurations, and it was extended to possibly non-finitely generated filtration in \cite{Sze15}. However, as pointed out in \cite{Nys12}, it is difficult to define the generalized Futaki invariants this way, and the definition in \cite[Def. 4]{Sze15} does not behave well e.g., it could change after taking a truncation. It also relates to \cite[Conj. 2.5]{BoJ18} from the non-Archimedean geometry.

\label{t-reducedK}
Notation as above. Let $T\subset \operatorname{Aut}(X)$ be a maximal torus. Then the followings are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (reduced uniform K-stablity) there exists some $\eta>0$, such that for any $({\mathcal{X}};{\mathcal{L}})$, 
$${\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}};{\mathcal{L}})\ge \eta\cdot  \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{NA}}_{T}({\mathcal{X}};{\mathcal{L}});$$
\item (reduced uniform Ding-stablity) there exists some $\eta>0$, such that for any linearly bounded filtration $\mathcal{F}$,  
$$\mathbf{D}^{\mathrm{NA}}(\mathcal{F})\ge \eta\cdot  \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{NA}}_{T}(\mathcal{F});$$
\item there exists $\delta>1$ such that for any linearly bounded filtration $\mathcal{F}$, we can find $\xi\in N_{{\mathbb{R} }}$ such that $\beta_{X,\delta}(\mathcal{F}_{\xi})\ge 0$, 
\item $X$ is K-semistable and $\sup_{\xi\in N_{{\mathbb{R} }}}\beta_{X}(v_{\xi})> 0$ for any quasi-monomial $v$ which is not induced by the torus, 
\item $\delta_{T}(X)>1$. 
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: While it has been worked out in KSB theory for how to define a family of higher dimensional varieties, which in particular solves all the local issues on defining a family of Fano varieties, however, there are two main differences between moduli of Fano varieties and moduli of KSB-stable varieties: firstly, if we aim to find a compact moduli space of Fano varieties, we often have to add Fano varieties with infinite automorphism group, which is a phenomena that does not happen in the KSB moduli case; secondly, a more profound issue is that Minimal Model Program often provides more than one limit for a family of Fano varieties over a punctured curve, thus it is unclear how to find a MMP theory that picks the right limit. The second moduli problem is the one parametrizing (Gieseker) semistable sheaves on a polarized projective scheme (X,O_X(1)) with fixed Hilbert polynomial (see ).

We separate the proof into a few steps.
\medskip

\noindent{\it Step 1: Defining the filtrations.}


Let  $\pi: X \to C$ and  $\pi': X'\to C$
 be ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Gorenstein families of  $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties over a smooth pointed curve $0 \in C$.  
Assume there exists an isomorphism 
\[
\phi: X \times_C C^\circ  \to X' \times_C C^\circ
\] 
over $C^\circ: C\setminus \{0 \}$ that does not extend to an isomorphism $X \simeq X'$ over $C$. 
After shrinking, we may assume $C$ is affine and there exists a local uniformizer $t$. 

 From this setup, we will construct filtrations on the section rings of the special fibers. 
Set 
\[L := -rK_X
\quad \text{ and } \quad
L':=-rK_{X'},
\]
where $r$ is a positive integer so that $L$ and $L'$ are Cartier. 
For each non-negative integer $m$, set
\begin{align*}
{\mathcal{R}}_m &:=H^0(X, {\mathcal{O}}_X(mL))   
 & {\mathcal{R}}'_{m} &:=  H^0(X', {\mathcal{O}}_X(mL') )\\
R_m &:= H^0(X_0,  {\mathcal{O}}_X(mL_0) )
& R'_m&:= H^0(X'_0, {\mathcal{O}}_X(mL_0) ). 
\end{align*} 
Additionally, set  
$${\mathcal{R}}:= \displaystyle  \oplus_{ m} {\mathcal{R}}_m, 
\quad 
R:= \displaystyle  \oplus_{ m} R_m,
\quad
{\mathcal{R}}':= \displaystyle  \oplus_{ m} {\mathcal{R}}'_m, 
\quad \text{ and } \quad 
R': = \displaystyle \oplus_{ m} R'_m.$$

Fix a common log resolution $\widehat{X}$ of $X$ and $X'$ 
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
  & \widehat{X}  \arrow[dr, "\psi'"] \arrow[dl,swap,"\psi"]& \\
  X  \arrow[rr, dashrightarrow, "\phi"] & & X'
   \end{tikzcd} 
   \end{center}
   and write $\widetilde{X_0}$ and $\widetilde{X'_0}$ for the birational transforms of $X_0$ and $X'_0$ on $\widehat{X}$. 
 Set 
 \begin{eqnarray}\label{e-defa}
a: = A_{X,X_0}(\widetilde{X'_0}) \mbox{\ \ \ and \ \ \ }a' := A_{X', X'_0 }(\widetilde{X_0}).
\end{eqnarray}
Observe that  $\widetilde{X_0}\neq \widetilde{X'_0}$, since otherwise $\phi$ would extend to an isomorphism over $C$ as $-K_{X}$ and $-K_{X'}$ are ample. Moreover, $a, a'>0$ since $X_0$ and $X_0'$ are klt, and we can apply inversion of adjunction. 

For each $p\in {\mathbb{Z} }$ and $m\in {\mathbb{N}}$, set
  \[
  \mathcal{F}^p {\mathcal{R}}_m:= \{ s\in  {\mathcal{R}}_m \, \vert \, {\rm ord}_{\widetilde{X'_0}} (s) \geq p \},  \mbox{\ \ and \ \ }
    \mathcal{F}'^p {\mathcal{R}}'_m := \{ s\in {\mathcal{R}}_m \, \vert \, {\rm ord}_{\widetilde{X_0}} (s) \geq p \}
    .\]
We define filtrations of $R$ and $R'$ by setting 
\[
\mathcal{F}^{p} R_m : = {\rm im}( \mathcal{F}^p {\mathcal{R}}_m \to R_m) 
 \mbox{\ \ and \ \ }
\mathcal{F}'^{p} R'_m : = {\rm im}( \mathcal{F}'^p {\mathcal{R}}'_m  \to R'_m),
\]
where the previous maps are given by restriction of sections.  It is straightforward to check that $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{F}'$ are filtrations of $R$ and $R'$. 

Note that a section $s \in R_m$ lies in $\mathcal{F}^p R_m$  if and only if there exists an extension $\tilde{s} \in {\mathcal{R}}_m$ of $s$ such that $\tilde{s} \in  \mathcal{F}^p {\mathcal{R}}_m$. The analogous statement holds for $\mathcal{F}'$.

\medskip

\noindent{\it Step 2: Relating the filtrations.}

 Since $p^*(X_0) = q^*(X'_0)$ have multiplicity one along $\widetilde{X_0}$ and $\widetilde{X'_0}$, we may write 
\[
K_{ \widehat{X}}  = \psi^*(K_X)  + a \widetilde{X'_0} +  F    \mbox{\ \ and \ \ }
K_{ \widehat{X}}  = \psi'^*(K_{X'})  + a' \widetilde{X_0} + F',
\]
where the components of ${\rm Supp}(F) \cup {\rm Supp}(F')$ are both $\psi$- and $\psi'$-exceptional. 
Now,
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{F}^p {\mathcal{R}}_m& \simeq H^0\Big(
\widehat{X},{\mathcal{O}}_{\widehat{X}} \big(m \psi^* L -p \widetilde{X'_0} \big)\Big)  \\
	&= H^0 \left(
	\widehat{X}, {\mathcal{O}}_{\widehat{X}} \big(m \psi'^*L' +(mra- p )\widetilde{X'_0}- mra' \widetilde{X_0}+mr(F-F' ) \big) 
	\right). 
\end{align*}
Hence, for $s\in \mathcal{F}^p  {\mathcal{R}}_m$, multiplying $\psi^*s$ by $t^{mra -p}$ gives an element of 
\[
H^0 \Big(\widehat{X},{\mathcal{O}}_{\widehat{X}}\big(m\psi'^*L'  -( mr(a+a')- p) \widetilde{X_0}\big) \Big),\]
which can be identified with  $\mathcal{F}^{mr(a+a')-p}{\mathcal{R}}'_m$. 

As described above, for each $p\in {\mathbb{Z} }$ and $m\in {\mathbb{N}}$, there is a map
 \[\varphi_{p,m}:
\mathcal{F}^{p}{\mathcal{R}}_m \longrightarrow 
\mathcal{F}^{mr(a+a')-p} {\mathcal{R}}'_m
,\]
which, when  ${\mathcal{R}}_m$ and ${\mathcal{R}}'_m$ are viewed as submodules of $K(X)=K(X')$,  sends $s\in \mathcal{F}^{p}{\mathcal{R}}_m$ to $t^{mra-p}({\phi^{-1}})^*(s)$. 
 Similarly, there is a map 
 \[\varphi'_{p,m}:
\mathcal{F}^{p} {\mathcal{R}}'_m \longrightarrow 
\mathcal{F}^{mr(a+a')-p} {\mathcal{R}}_m
,\]
which sends $s' \in \mathcal{F}^{p} {\mathcal{R}}'_m$ to $t^{mra'-p}\phi^*(s')$.


\begin{lem}\label{l-Fcompare}
The map $\varphi_{p,m}$ is an isomorphism. Furthermore, given $s\in \mathcal{F}^{p} {\mathcal{R}}_m$
\begin{itemize}
\item[(1)] $s$ vanishes on $X_0$ if and only if $\varphi_{p,m}(s) \in \mathcal{F}'^{mr(a+a')-p+1} {\mathcal{R}}'_m$, and
\item[(2)]    $\varphi_{p,m}(s)$ vanishes on $X'_0$ if and only if $s\in \mathcal{F}^{p+1} {\mathcal{R}}_m$.
\end{itemize}
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
The map $\varphi'_{mr(a+a')-p,m}$ is the inverse to $\varphi_{p,m}$, since
 $\varphi'_{mr(a+a')-p,m}\circ \varphi_{p,m}$ is multiplication by $t^{mra'-(mr(a+a')-p) }t^{mra-p}=1$. 
 Hence, $\varphi_{p,m}$ is an isomorphism. 
 
For (1), fix $s\in \mathcal{F}^{p} {\mathcal{R}}_m$ and note that $s$ vanishes on $X_0$ if and only if 
$$
\psi^*s \in H^0\Big(\widehat{X}, {\mathcal{O}}_{\widehat{X}} \big( m \psi^* L -p \widetilde{X'_0} -  \widetilde{X_0} \big) \Big)
.$$
 The latter holds precisely when
  \[t^{mra-b}\psi^*s
  \in H^0\Big(
  \widehat{X}, {\mathcal{O}}_{\widehat{X}} \big(m \psi'^* L' - (mr(a+a')-p +1) \widetilde{X_0} \big)\Big),\]
 which is identified with $\mathcal{F}'^{mr(a+a')-p +1 }{\mathcal{R}};_m$. Statement (2) follows from a similar argument. 
 \end{proof}
 
 
 \begin{prop}\label{p-isomgrF}
 The maps $(\varphi_{p,m})$ induce an isomorphism of graded rings 
 \begin{eqnarray}\label{e-graded}
\bigoplus_{ m\in {\mathbb{N}}  }  \bigoplus_{p\in \mathbb{Z} }{\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}}^p R_m 
\overset{\varphi}{\longrightarrow}
 \bigoplus_{m \in {\mathbb{N}} } \bigoplus_{p \in \mathbb{Z}} {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}'}^{p}R'_m ,
 \end{eqnarray}
that sends the degree $(m,p)$-summand on the left to the degree $(m,mr(a+a')-p)$-summand on the right. 
Hence, 
 $ {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}}^p R_m$ and ${\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}'}^p R'_m$ vanish for $p>mr(a+a')$. 
 \end{prop}

   
   \begin{proof}
Consider the map
   \begin{equation}\label{e-FF'}
   \mathcal{F}^p R_m \longrightarrow {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}'}^{mr(a+a')-p} R'_m. 
   \end{equation}
 defined as follows.
Given an element of $s\in \mathcal{F}^p R_m$, choose $\tilde{s} \in \mathcal{F}^p {\mathcal{R}}_m$ such that $\tilde{s}$ is an extension of $s$. 
Now, send $s$ to the image of $\varphi_{p,m}(\tilde{s})$ under the composition of maps 
\[
\mathcal{F}'^{mr(a+a') - p } {\mathcal{R}}'_m \to \mathcal{F}'^{mr(a+a') - p } R'_m \to {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}'}^{mr(a+a')-p} R'_m.
\]
This map can be easily seen well defined.

Using Lemma \ref{l-Fcompare}, we see that \eqref{e-FF'} is surjective and has its kernel equal to $\mathcal{F}^{p+1} R_m$. Indeed, the surjectivity follows from the fact that $\varphi_{p,m}$ is an isomorphism. The description of the kernel is a consequence of Lemma \ref{l-Fcompare}.2. Therefore, 
$${\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}}^p R_m \to {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}'}^{mr(a+a')-p} R'_m$$ 
is an isomorphism. The previous  isomorphism induces an isomorphism of graded rings, since $\varphi_{p_1,m_1}(s_1)  \varphi_{p_2,m_2}(s_2)  = \varphi_{p_1+p_2,m_1+m_2}(s_1  s_2)$ for $s_1\in \mathcal{F}^{p_1}{\mathcal{R}}_{m_1}$ and $s_2 \in \mathcal{F}^{p_2} {\mathcal{R}}_{m_2}$.  

To see the vanishing statement, observe that 
 $ {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}}^p R_m$ and ${\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}}'^pR'_m$ vanish for $p<0$. Hence, the isomorphism of graded rings yields the 
 vanishing for $p>mr(a+a')$. 
 \end{proof}



\begin{rem}\label{r-filtrationcoincide}
The above filtration defined in \cite{BX19} was trying to extend the filtration defined in \cite{BHJ17} (see the proof of  Lemma \ref{l-beta=w}) for test configurations into a more general relative setting. 
In hindsight, this indeed coincides with the canonical filtration introduced in \cite{AHH18} when considering $S$-completeness for vector bundles (see \cite{AHH18}*{Rem. 3.36}). \end{rem}

The connection between the above filtration with K-stability can be seen by the following statement.



\begin{prop}\label{p-TSa}Let 
\[
\beta=ar^n(-K_{X_0})^n-\int^{\infty}_{0} {\rm vol}(\mathcal{F}^tR) dt \mbox{\  and \  } \beta'=a'r^n(-K_{X'_0})^n-\int^{\infty}_{0} {\rm vol}(\mathcal{F}'^tR') dt
\]
Then
$\beta + \beta' = 0$ .
\end{prop}

\begin{proof}
Applying Proposition \ref{p-isomgrF}, we see 
\begin{align*}
\dim \mathcal{F}^p R_m = \sum_{j=p}^{mr(a+a')} {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}}^j R_m 
			&= \sum_{j=0}^{mr(a+a')-p} {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}'}^{j} R'_m \\
			& = \dim R_m  - \dim \mathcal{F}^{mr(a+a')-p+1}R'_m ,
\end{align*} 
for  $p \in \{0, \ldots , mr(a+a')+1\}$.
Therefore, 
\[
\sum_{p=0 }^{mr(a+a')} \dim \mathcal{F}^p R_m
+
\sum_{p=0 }^{mr(a+a')} \dim \mathcal{F}'^p R'_m
=mr(a+a') \dim R_m
.\]
Then we conclude by dividing both sides by $\frac{1}{n!}m^{n+1}$ and let $m\to \infty$.  \end{proof}

 
Let ${\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F})$ be the base ideal sequences for $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$, i.e., ${\mathfrak{a}}_{p}={\mathfrak{a}}_p({\rm ord}_{\widetilde{X'_0}})$;  and ${\mathfrak{b}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F})$ the restriction of ${\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F})$ on  $X_0$.  Then the inversion of adjunction implies that
${\rm lct}(X,X_0; {\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}))={\rm lct}(X_0;{\mathfrak{b}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}))$. Since we have $a\ge {\rm lct}(X,X_0; {\mathfrak{a}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}))$ and ${\mathfrak{b}}_{p}\supset I_{m,p}:=I_{m,p}(\mathcal{F})$ (see Definition \ref{defn:D^NA} for the definition of $I_{m,p}$) for any $m$ (and the equality holds for $m\gg 0$), we have
 $$a\ge {\rm lct}(X_0;{\mathfrak{b}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}))\ge \mu_{X_0}(\mathcal{F}).$$
 Similarly, we can define  and get $a'\ge {\rm lct}(X'_0;{\mathfrak{b}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}'))\ge \mu_{X'_0}(\mathcal{F}')$.  Now since $X_0$ and $X'_0$ are K-semistable, and $\beta\ge \beta_{X_0}(\mathcal{F})\ge 0$ and $\beta'\ge 0$. Thus $\beta = \beta'=0$ and $a= {\rm lct}(X_0;{\mathfrak{b}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}))= \mu_{X_0}(\mathcal{F})$, $a'= {\rm lct}(X'_0;{\mathfrak{b}}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}'))= \mu_{X'_0}(\mathcal{F}')$.

 
 \medskip
 
 \noindent{\it Step 3: Finite generations.}
 
 The remaining part of the proof is to show that the graded ring in \eqref{e-graded} is finitely generated and yields normal test configurations, since then by \cite{LX14}, this will imply that the Proj of the graded ring yields a 
K-semistable $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano variety.  In \cite{BX19}, this is  the most involving part of the proof, using the cone construction.  
Based on a better understanding of filtrations for K-stability problems, 
now we have an argument which significantly simplifies the technical one in \cite{BX19} as follows, though the underlying strategy remains the same. \footnote{This argument is suggested by Harold Blum.}

We know that there is a sufficiently large $m$ and sufficiently small $\epsilon$, such that ${\rm lct}(X,X_0;\frac{1}{m}I_{m,(a-\epsilon)m})\ge 1$. Thus for a general divisor $D\in \mathcal{F}^{(a-\epsilon)m}{\mathcal{R}}_m$,  $(X,X_0+\frac{1}{mr}D)$ is log canonical. On the other hand,
$$A_{X,X_0+\frac{1}{mr}D}(\widetilde{X'_0})=a-\frac{1}{mr}{\rm ord}_{X_0'}(D)\le \epsilon.$$

Thus from \cite{BCHM10}, we know that there exists a model $\mu\colon Z\to X$, which precisely extract $X_0'$, and 
the ring 
$$\bigoplus_{m\in \mathbb N}\bigoplus_{p\in \mathbb N}H^0(Z,\mu^*(-mrK_X)-pX_0')$$ 
is finitely generated. Its restriction on $R$ yields $\oplus_p\mathcal{F}^pR$, which is finitely generated and the graded ring in \eqref{e-graded} yields test configurations $Y$ and $Y'$ of $X_0$ and $X_0'$.
\begin{claim} $Y$ and $Y'$ are normal test configurations. 
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}To see the claim, we want to use the construction in \ref{sss-Scompleteness}. We know that the above argument yields a family 
$$ \mathsf{X}:={\rm Proj}\bigoplus_m\big(i_*(\pi^{\circ}_*(-rmK_{ \mathsf{X}^{\circ}}))\big)$$
over $\overline{\rm ST}(R)$ (see \eqref{e-STR}). Then the two test configurations $Y$ (resp. $Y'$) are given by $s=0$ (resp. $t=0$). Denote by $\mathsf D$ the closure of $D$ on $\mathsf X$. Since  $\phi$ yields a family $\pi^{\circ}\colon \mathsf{X}^{\circ}\to \overline{\rm ST}(R)\setminus 0$, which is normal, and $ \mathsf{X}\setminus \mathsf{X}^{\circ}$ is of codimension 2, we conclude that $\mathsf{X}$ is normal. 
We consider $\mathsf{X}'$ the family over $\overline{\rm ST}(R)$ obtained by the trivial isomorphism $X\to X$, and $\mathsf{D}'$ the divisor on $ \mathsf{X}'$ which is obtained by gluing $D$ on $X$ using the trivial isomorphism. In particular,  $(\mathsf X', \frac 1m\mathsf D')$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-Gorenstein family of log canonical CYs over $\overline{\rm ST}(R)$. 

On $\mathsf X'$,  $t=0$ and $s=0$ are two divisors $Z$ and $Z'$ (isomorphic to $X_0\times \mathbb{A}^1$). Let 
$$\epsilon':=A_{\mathsf X',\frac 1m \mathsf  D'+Z+Z'}(Y')=A_{X,\frac 1mD+X_0}(\widetilde{X'_0})\le \epsilon,$$
then $(\mathsf X,\frac 1m \mathsf  D+Y+(1-\epsilon')Y')$ is crepant birationally equivalent to $(\mathsf X',\frac 1m \mathsf  D'+Z+Z')$, which in particular implies that $(\mathsf X,Y+(1-\epsilon')Y')$ is log canonical. 
As $\epsilon'\to 0$, we know $(\mathsf X,Y+Y')$ is log canonical, which implies $Y$ and $Y'$ are normal.
\end{proof}
Since $0=\beta(\mathcal{F})\ge {\rm Ding}(Y)$ by Theorem \ref{t-betading}, it implies ${\rm Ding}(Y)=0$. Thus $Y$ is a special test configuration by Theorem \ref{t-specialdegeneration}, and the special fiber $Y_0$ is K-semistable (see \cite[Lemma 3.1]{LWX18}). Similarly, $X_0'$ degenerates $Y_0$ via the special test configuration $Y'$.

 defined as follows.

 $ {\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}}^p R_m$ and ${\rm gr}_{\mathcal{F}}'^pR'_m$ vanish for $p<0$. Hence, the isomorphism of graded rings yields the 
 vanishing for $p>mr(a+a')$.

Denote by $k$ the residue field of $R$.
Let 
$${\mathcal{R}}:=\bigoplus_m {\mathcal{R}}_m=\bigoplus_mH^0(X_R, -rmK_{X_R})$$ for a sufficiently divisible $r$.
The special test configuration ${\mathcal{X}}_{\eta}$ induces a special divisor $E_{\eta}$, which yields a filtration $ \mathcal{F}_{\eta}:=\mathcal{F}_{E_{\eta}}$ on $R_{K}={\mathcal{R}}\otimes K(R)$.  For each $m$ and $i$, there is a unique extension of $ \mathcal{F}^{i}{\mathcal{R}}_m\subset {\mathcal{R}}_m$ of $\mathcal{F}^{i}_{\eta}(R_K)_m$ as an $R$-submodule, such that  $ {\mathcal{R}}_m/\mathcal{F}^i{\mathcal{R}}_m$ is a free $R$-module. Denote  by $\mathcal{F}_k^{\bullet}R_k$ the restricting filtration of $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ on $R_k={\mathcal{R}}\otimes k$, i.e. 
$$\mathcal{F}_k^iR_k={\rm Im}(\mathcal{F}^i{\mathcal{R}}_k\to {\mathcal{R}}_k\to R_k).$$  Then $\mathcal{F}_k^{\bullet}$ yields a multiplicative filtration on $R_k$.

Since ${\rm Fut}({\mathcal{X}}_{\eta})=0$, $\mu_{\mathcal{F}_{\eta}}=S(\mathcal{F}_{\eta})$. On the other hand, we have $\mu_{\mathcal{F}_k}\le \mu_{\mathcal{F}_{\eta}}$ and $S(\mathcal{F}_k)=S(\mathcal{F}_{\eta})$, we have $\mu_{\mathcal{F}_k}\le S(\mathcal{F}_k)$, which implies $\mu_{\mathcal{F}_k}=S(\mathcal{F}_k)$ as $X_k$ is K-semistable (see Theorem \ref{t-maintheorem2}). In particular, $\mu_{\mathcal{F}_{\eta}}=\mu_{\mathcal{F}_k}$. 

Then we can mimic the proof of Step 3 of Theorem \ref{t-main} to produce a test configuration ${\mathcal{X}}$ which extends ${\mathcal{X}}_K$ as follows. For any arbitrary positive $\epsilon$, we can find a divisor $D\in H^0(X_R, -rmK_{X_R})$  such that $(X_R, X_k+\frac{1}{mr}D)$ is a log canonical pair and $A_{X_{\eta},\frac{1}{mr}D_{\eta}}(E_{\eta})<\epsilon$. From this, we can easily conclude that the closure $E_R$ of $E_{\eta}$ is a dreamy divisor over $X_R$, whose induced filtration coincides with $\mathcal{F}$.  Therefore, we can produce such a test configuration ${\mathcal{X}}$.

Let $f : X \to T$ be a
proper flat morphism of varieties of relative dimension $n$ such that the general fiber is normal, and $L$ an $f$-ample ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Cartier divisor on $X$. 
Consider the Mumford-Knudsen expansion of ${\mathcal{O}}_X(rL)$ for a sufficiently divisible $r$:
$$ {\rm det} f_*({\mathcal{O}}_X (qrL)) \cong \bigotimes^{n+1}_{i=0}{\mathcal{M}}^{(^q_i)}_i$$
where $M_i$ are uniquely determined bundles on $T$. 

We define {\it the CM line bundle} to be  
$$\lambda_{f,rL}:= {\mathcal{M}}_{n+1}^{n(n+1)+\mu(rL)}\otimes{\mathcal{M}}_n^{-2(n+1)},$$
where $\mu(rL)=\frac{-nK_{X_t}\cdot (rL_t)^{n-1}}{(rL_t)^n}$ for a general fiber $X_t$, and $\lambda_{f,L}:=\frac{1}{r^n}\lambda_{f,rL}$ as a ${\mathbb{Q}}$-line bundle. It clearly does not depend on the choice of $r$. 

If both $X$ and $T$ are normal and projective, we can write it as an intersection
$$\lambda_{f,L} := f_*\big(\mu(L)\cdot L^{n+1}+ (n + 1)L^n\cdot K_{X/T}\big),$$
and if $L=-K_{X/T}$, we denote $\lambda_{f}:=-f_*(-K_{X/T})^{n+1}$. 

When $T=\mathfrak X^{\rm Kss}_{n,V}$ and $X\to T$ is the universal family, we can descend $\Lambda_{\rm CM}$ to get the CM (${\mathbb{Q}}$)-line bundle on $T=\mathfrak X^{\rm Kss}_{n,V}$, and one can show that $\lambda_{\rm CM}$ can be descent to $X^{\rm Kps}_{n,V}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
We give a sketch of the main ingredients in the proof.

\medskip


 \noindent{\it Step 1: Harder-Narashimhan filtration.}

Consider a family of ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Fano varieties $f\colon X\to C$ over a smooth projective curve. One remarkable idea in \cite{CP18} is to relate the positivity of $\lambda_f$ to the  Harder-Narashimhan filtration of $f_*(-mrK_{X/C})$. This becomes more transparent in \cite{XZ19}. One can consider the Harder-Narasimhan filtration $\mathcal{F}^i_{\rm HN}$ of the $\mathcal{O}_C$-algebra ${\mathcal{R}}:=\bigoplus_m f_*(-mrK_{X/C})$, where $\mathcal{F}^{\lambda}_{\rm HN}\subset f_*(-mrK_{X/C})$ is defined to be the union of all subbundles with slope at least $\lambda$. Restricting to a fiber $X_0$, and putting all $\lambda$ and $m$ together, we obtain {\it the Harder-Narashimhan filtration $\mathcal{F}^{\lambda}_{\rm HN}$} on $R=\bigoplus_{m\in {\mathbb{N} }}H^0(-mrK_{X_0})$, which can be easily proved to be a multiplicative linearly bounded filtration. 

 In \cite{CP18},  the proof uses the characterization of $\delta$-invariants as the limit of the log canonical thresholds of basis type divisors (see Equation \eqref{e-delta}). In \cite{XZ19}, we turned their argument into an inequality $\deg(\lambda_{f})\ge \beta(\mathcal{F}_{\rm HN})$, which is equivalent to saying $\mu_{X_0}(\mathcal{F}_{\rm HN})\le 0$. 
 In fact, for any $t> 0$ and any section of $D_0\in \mathcal{F}^{tm}_{\rm HN}R_m$ (for $m$ sufficiently large with $tm\ge 2g+1$) can be extended to a section 
 $$D\in |-rmK_{X/C}-f^*P|.$$ Therefore $(X_0,\frac{1}{mr}D_0)$ can not be log canonical since otherwise $ K_{X/C}+D\sim_{{\mathbb{Q}}} -\frac{1}{mr}f^*P$ and the pushforward of its multiple would violate the semi-positivity of the pushforward of the log canonical class. This implies that the log canonical slope $\mu_{X_0}(\mathcal{F}_{\rm HN})\le 0$. 

\medskip

\noindent {\it Step 2: Twist the family.}

This is an extra step which is special for a family of reduced uniformly K-stable ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Fano varieties, i.e., when there is a positive dimensional torus acting fiberwisely on the family. 
 
Let $f\colon X\to C$ be a ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Gorenstein family of ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Fano varieties $f\colon X\to C$ where a general fiber is reduced uniformly K-stable with respect to a torus $T$. Fixed a general fiber $X_t$. Then there exists a $\delta>1$ which only depends on $X_t$ such that for the Harder-Narashimhan filtration  $\mathcal{F}_{\rm HN}$, by Theorem \ref{t-reducedK} there exists a twist $\xi$ such that $\beta_{\delta}((\mathcal{F}_{\rm HN})_{\xi})\ge 0$. A somewhat subtle property is such $\xi$ can be chosen to be in $N(T)_{{\mathbb{Q}}}$ (see \cite[Proposition 5.6]{XZ19}). After a further finite base change $C'\to C$, we can assume $\xi\in N(T)$.
Consider 
$${\mathcal{R}}:=\bigoplus_{m\in {\mathbb{N} }}{\mathcal{R}}_m=\bigoplus_{m\in {\mathbb{N} }}f_*(-mrK_{X/C})$$
which can be decomposed into weight spaces
$${\mathcal{R}}:=\bigoplus_{m\in {\mathbb{N} }}{\mathcal{R}}_m=\bigoplus_{m\in {\mathbb{N} },\alpha\in M}{\mathcal{R}}_{m,\alpha}.$$
Now we can pick up any point $c\in C$, and construct the twisting family $f_{\xi}\colon X_{\xi}:={\rm Proj}_C({\mathcal{R}}_{\xi})\to C$ where
${\mathcal{R}}_{\xi}=\bigoplus_{m\in {\mathbb{N} },\alpha\in M}{\mathcal{R}}_{m,\alpha}\otimes \mathcal{O}_{C}(\langle \xi,\alpha \rangle\cdot c).$ It is easy to check $\lambda_{f}\sim_{{\mathbb{Q}}}\lambda_{f_{\xi}}$  as a general fiber is K-semistable, and the Harder-Narashimhan filtration of the twisting family $f_{\xi}\colon X_{\xi}\to C$ is $(\mathcal{F}_{\rm HN})_{\xi}$ (see \cite[Corollary 5.3]{XZ19}).

Then from $\beta_{\delta}((\mathcal{F}_{\rm HN})_{\xi})\ge 0$, we can show $-K_{X_{\xi}/C}+\frac{\delta}{(n+1)(-K_X)^n(\delta-1)}f^*_{\xi}(\lambda_f)$ is nef (see \cite[Proposition 4.9]{XZ20}).

\medskip

\noindent{\it Step 3: Ampleness lemma.}

In this step we want to show that if there is a ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Gorenstein family $f\colon X\to T$ of ${\mathbb{Q}}$-Fano varieties with maximal variation such that general fibers are reduced uniformly K-stable,  then $\lambda_{f}$ is big.
By \cite{BDPP13}, it suffices to show that there exists an ${\mathbb{Q}}$-ample line bundle $H$ such that for any covering family of curves $\{C\}$ of $T$, $\lambda_{f}\cdot C\ge H\cdot C$.

Using Koll\'ar's ampleness lemma in \cite{Kol90, KP17} and the product trick, it is shown in \cite{CP18} that this is true if there is a uniform constant $c$ such that $-K_{X_C/C}+c f^*\lambda_{f}$ is nef. (Moreover, they show  if $X_t$ is uniformly K-stable, such uniform constant $M$ exists.) 

In our case, applying the construction of the Step 2,  we can twist the family to get  $X_{C,\xi}\to C$ such that $\beta_{\delta}((\mathcal{F}_{\rm HN})_{\xi})\ge 0$ for a uniform constant $\delta>1$ (see Theorem \ref{t-reducedK}), which only depends on $X/C$. Then we can take $c=\frac{\delta}{(n+1)(-K_X)^n(\delta-1)}$ and we know that $-K_{X_{C,\xi}/C}+c f^*\lambda_{f}$ is nef.

To conclude, we have to track the proof of the ampleness lemma to strengthen it to a version that includes all twists. For more details, see \cite[Section 6]{XZ19}.

nodes.name: Case of log pairs
nodes.statement: Unlike Part , in various steps of the moduli theory, to treat the case of log pairs could post substantial new difficulty. Among them, maybe the most difficult one is to give an appropriate definition of a family of log pairs over a general base. This is settled in , by considering K-flat pairs over the base. While to generalize the boundedness and openness to the log pair case, the argument is essentially the same. To get the good moduli space, extra care has to been took for the subtle degeneration behaviour for the divisors. And for projectivity, it needs one more step to get the positivity of the CM line bundle from the ampleness lemma. In the KSB case, this is worked out in . For K-moduli, see and *Sec. 7.

If $X$ is not K-stable, then we know there exists a divisor $E$ over $X$ such that $\delta(E)=\delta(X)=1$. We want to show that this implies $X\cong \mathbb{P}^1$.

Consider the restricted volume function 
\[
Q:=-\frac{1}{n}\frac{d}{dt}{\rm vol}(-\mu^*K_X-tE)dt \mbox{ \ \ for } t\in [0,\tau),\]
 where $\tau:=\tau(E)$ is the pseudo-effective threshold of $E$ with respect to $-K_X$. The main property we need about $Q$ is that  it is a concave function which follows from that it is equal to the restricted volume and the latter is log concave (see \cite{ELMNP09}). Moreover, $Q$ is smooth on $[0,\tau)$ and can be extended to a continuous function on $[0,\tau]$.
We have
 \begin{eqnarray}
 \frac{\int^{\tau}_0 tQdt}{\int^{\tau}_0Q dt}=\frac{\frac{1}{n}\int^{\tau}_{0}{\rm vol}(\mu^*(-K_X)-tE)dt}{\frac{1}{n}(-K_X)^n}=S_X(E)=A_{X}(E)\ge\frac{n}{n+1}\tau,
 \end{eqnarray}
  as $\beta(E)=0$ and $\alpha(X)=\frac{n}{n+1}$. We denote by $A:=A_{X}(E)$.
  
  By the concavity, we know that $Q(t)\ge (\frac{t}{A})^{n-1}Q(A)$ for $t\in [0,A]$ and $Q(t)\le (\frac{t}{A})^{n-1}Q(A)$ for $t\in [A,\tau].$
  So 
  \begin{eqnarray*}
  0&=&\int^{\tau}_{0}(t-A)Q(t)dt\\
  &\le& Q(A)\int^{\tau}_{0}(t-A)(\frac{t}{A})^{n-1}dt\\
  &=&\frac{Q(A) \tau^n}{A^{n-1}}(\frac{\tau}{n+1}-\frac{A}{n})\\
  &\le &0.
  \end{eqnarray*}
This implies that $A=\frac{n}{n+1}\tau$ and $Q(t)= (\frac{t}{A})^{n-1}Q(A)$ for $t\in[0,\tau]$.

To proceed, since $E$ computes $\delta(X)=1$, we know we can find a model $\mu\colon Y\to X$ only extracting $E$, so we know that for $t\ll 1$,
$$Q=-\frac{1}{n}\frac{d}{dt}{\rm vol}(-\mu^*K_X-t E)|_{t=t_0}=E\cdot(-\mu^*K_X-tE)^{n-1}.$$
Compared to $Q(t)= (\frac{t}{A})^{n-1}Q(A)$, we know $E^i\cdot (\mu^*K_X)^{n-i}=0$ and all $0\le i \le n-1$, which in particular implies $E$ is mapped to a point.   Moreover, $Q=t^{n-1}(-E|_E)^{n-1}$, which implies for $t\in [0,\tau]$,
$${\rm vol}(-K_X-tE)=n\int^{\tau}_{t}Qdu=(\tau^n-t^n)E(-E)^{n-1}=(-K_X)^n-t^nE(-E)^{n-1}.$$
 This implies $\tau=\epsilon$, which is the nef threshold of $E$ with respect to $-K_X$. 
 
 
  
  Since $E$ is dreamy by Theorem \ref{t-delta=1}, we know $\mu^*(-K_X)-\tau E$ is semi-ample but not big. Since $\mu^*(-K_X)-\tau E$ is ample on $E$, we know a sufficiently divisible multiple of $\mu^*(-K_X)-\tau E$ will give a fibration struction $\rho\colon Y\to Z$, whose restrict on $E$ is finite. Thus a general fiber of $\rho$ is a curve $l$. Since $Y$ is normal, $l$ is in the smooth locus. Thus $K_Y\cdot l=-2$ and $0=(\mu^*(-K_X)-\tau E)\cdot l=2-(1+\frac{1}{n+1}\tau) E\cdot l$, which implies $E\cdot l=1$, $\tau=n+1$ and $A=n$. So $Y\to X$ is the blow up of the smooth point, and we know the Seshadri constant at this point is $n+1$, therefore $X\cong \mathbb{P}^n$ by \cite{LZ18}. Then $\alpha(\mathbb{P}^n)=\frac{1}{n+1}$.

nodes.statement: The K\"ahler-Einstein problem for smooth del Pezzo surfaces has been completely answered by Tian . So it is natural to take a look at all smooth Fano threefolds which are classified by Iskovskih when rho(X)=1 (see ) and Mori-Mukai when rho(X)ge 2 (see ). When rho(X)=1, there are nineteen families. Among them, the one with genus 12 (i.e. (-K_X)^3=22) which contains the famous Mukai-Umemura manifold has attract lots of interests (see for recent progress). Let r(X):=\r | -K_Xsim -rH, mbox for H generator of Pic(X) \ be the Fano index. There are seven families with r(X)ge 2 and they are all known to be K-polystable or K-stable. It is tempting to speculate All smooth Fano threefolds with rho(X)=1 are K-semistable. Using the classification of smooth Fano threefolds, it is indeed an active research topic to completely determine all their K-(semi,poly)stability. For rho(X)ge 2, in , beta-invariants for divisors on X itself are computed, and many cases are shown to be K-unstable. For Fano threefolds with rho(X)=1 and r(X)=1, it will be very interesting to connect various compactifications of moduli of K3 surfaces of genus g (1le g le 10 and g=12) and the K-moduli of the corresponding Fano threefolds with the volume 2g-2, i.e. to extend the well studied correspondence to the boundary of the moduli spaces. The higher dimensional analogue of Conjecture , as originally proposed in which predicted that smooth Picard number 1 Fano manifolds in any dimension are K-semistable, was disproved in , where it is shown that a del Pezzo manifold X of degree five with dimension four or five are K-unstable.
